claims.text: Introducing a controlled grain-size gradient simultaneously improves strength and ductility.
Surface mechanical attrition or another severe-plastic-deformation technique can create a nano-grained surface layer transitioning to coarser grains in the core.
A grain-size gradient induces differential dislocation densities through the material thickness.
A grain-size gradient induces differential strain-hardening rates through the material thickness.
The fine-grained surface region provides high strength through dislocation blocking.
The fine-grained surface region provides high strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The coarser-grained interior preserves ductility because it has fewer grain boundaries.
Enhanced strain compatibility in the coarser-grained interior helps preserve ductility.
The gradient structure produces higher yield strength than a uniformly grained microstructure.
The gradient structure produces greater elongation before fracture than a uniformly grained microstructure.
A uniform micron-scale microstructure without a gradient has an inferior strength–ductility balance.
Achieving a stable gradient microstructure is necessary for the proposed mechanical response.
An excessively large grain-size gradient or an improper transition can reduce ductility.
Excessive deformation during processing can cause premature failure.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition, processing parameters, and extent of gradient refinement.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires improved elongation, whereas the falsification rule accepts merely comparable ductility as consistent with the hypothesis.

The stated baseline is a uniform micron-scale microstructure, but the experiment instead uses a uniformly fine-grained specimen as the control, so the proposed test does not directly evaluate the stated baseline comparison.
